brief: A worked example of every page type: a fictional regional rail operator, Northvale Rail, asks whether and how it can grow from 48 million to 60 million journeys a year by FY31. Every number is illustrative.
question: Can Northvale Rail grow from 48 million to 60 million journeys a year by FY31, and how?
answer: Northvale can reach 60 million journeys by FY31 by filling the off-peak rather than the full peak: add off-peak frequency first, electrify the Eastern line next and reform fares last.

cover.title: Northvale Rail: the road to 60 million journeys
cover.subtitle: Illustrative example: one worked page of every page type

slides.title: Northvale can reach 60 million journeys by FY31 by filling the off-peak
slides.highlight: frequency, not fares, is the main lever
points: Journeys recovered to 48.3 million in FY26 but growth slowed to 1.7%: peak trains run above 90% of their seats, so the peak cannot absorb the 11.7 million extra journeys.
Off-peak trains run at 38% of their seats. Half-hourly stations grew off-peak journeys 3.7 times as fast as hourly ones, so frequency, not fares, is the main lever.
Electrifying the Eastern line costs £390 million, beats bi-mode trains on cost per journey from year six and frees diesel units for the Dales line.
The £640 million plan pays back in eleven years on the central case, if the power upgrade lands by 2029 and punctuality holds at 90%.
Two of the seven 2027 milestones are at risk, both on the electrification path; the 5.1 million off-peak journeys depend on neither.

slides.title: Northvale sits mid-table on journeys per route-km, 27% below the leading peer

points.text: Northvale carries 104 thousand journeys per route-km, just under the peer median of 108 and 27% below Westmoor, the most intensive operator in the set.
Westmoor and Southdown run half-hourly off-peak services on most lines; Northvale runs hourly on three of its five, and its peak intensity is close to theirs.
Reaching the peer median off-peak intensity on the Dales and Valley lines alone would add about 7 million journeys a year on today's network.

slides.title: Leisure is two thirds of off-peak travel but only a seventh of the peak

exhibit.heading: Journeys by purpose and time band, FY26

points.text: Commuters are 68% of peak journeys but 18% of weekday off-peak journeys, where leisure trips make up two thirds of travel and business trips only 7%.
A leisure trip can go by car or not happen at all, so it responds to waiting time and reach far more than a commute does: lapsed leisure riders cite the wait twice as often as the fare.
Leisure is 88% of Saturday and 92% of Sunday journeys, yet Sunday runs the thinnest timetable of the week, with no train before 09:00 on three of the five lines.
Growth between the peaks is a leisure product: frequency, weekend service and destinations people want to reach, not a cheaper season ticket for the commuters who already travel.

slides.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 on-train survey, 11,400 responses

slides.title: Half-hourly off-peak stations grew off-peak journeys 3.7 times as fast as hourly ones

exhibit.heading: Off-peak service against off-peak journey growth, FY23-FY26

points.text: The six stations with 30 or more off-peak trains a weekday grew off-peak journeys by 16.5% on average over three years; the four stations still served hourly grew by 4.5%.
Population grew by 2-4% around all ten stations over the same period, so it cannot explain a gap of twelve points between the two groups.
Growth rises steeply up to about 30 trains a day and flattens after it: a half-hourly service is the threshold that matters, and more than that adds little off-peak demand.

slides.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; ticket sales by origin station

slides.title: Northvale's cost per train-km is ninth of twenty, £3.40 above the lowest-cost operator

points.text: At £17.60 per train-km Northvale sits just below the field's median of £18.10, and £3.40 above Westmoor, the lowest-cost operator.
Five of the six lowest-cost operators run electric trains on their busiest lines; every operator above £19.00 still runs diesel on most of its network.
Southdown carries almost as many journeys as Northvale at £2.30 less per train-km, because its units run 14 hours a day against Northvale's 11.
Electric trains on the Eastern line take Northvale to £16.40 by FY31, which would place it sixth of twenty on today's figures, level with Oakfield Link.

slides.title: Each peak train added to the Eastern line has cost a point of punctuality

exhibits.heading: Eastern line peak trains per hour

annotations.text: Four more peak trains an hour than in FY22
Lowest on the network, 5.1 points below FY22

points: Four extra peak trains an hour since FY22 have coincided with a 5.1-point fall in Eastern line punctuality: each added train leaves less recovery time at the two single-track sections east of Selby, so one late train now delays the next three.
Off-peak trains share none of that conflict, because the single-track sections are free for most of the hour between the peaks.
The plan therefore holds the peak timetable where it is and adds all its new service between the peaks, where it costs no punctuality.
slides.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; punctuality is arrivals within five minutes

slides.title: Four constraints hold the peak where it is: fleet, crews, track and depot

blocks.label: The fleet is fully used
points: All 58 units run in the morning peak and none is held spare, so a failure cancels a train rather than swapping in a replacement.
New units are on order but not before 2029, when electrification releases eleven diesel units for other lines.

blocks.label: Crews are fully rostered
points: Every peak diagram is covered, but 9% of peak shifts rely on rest-day overtime, so a new peak train would have no driver to run it.
Fourteen drivers in training qualify by mid-2027; the plan assigns them to the off-peak timetable, not to the peak.

metric.label: of peak shifts on rest-day overtime

blocks.label: Single track east of Selby
points: The Eastern line runs through two single-track sections where trains in opposite directions wait for each other.
Each extra peak train adds a crossing, which is why punctuality fell as the timetable grew.
Doubling both sections would cost about £38 million and is not in the funded plan.

metric.label: single-track sections on the Eastern line

blocks.label: The depot is almost full
points: The Dales depot stables trains overnight in 94% of its sidings, so no more units can be based there.
The planned extension adds twelve sidings for £55 million and is the one dependency of the off-peak timetable.

slides.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; fleet diagram, track layout and depot plan, FY26

slides.title: Frequency drives a loop: shorter waits win leisure trips that fund the next train
highlight: twice as often as the fare

points.text: Survey respondents who drove instead of taking the train cited the wait for the next service twice as often as the fare.
An added off-peak train on the Dales line covers its operating cost within 26 months once it carries 40 passengers a trip, and the average off-peak Dales train already carries 31.
It needs spare units and crews between the peaks; on the Coast line both are already committed until 2030, so the loop cannot start there before electrification releases diesel units.

slides.title: London and Manchester send three in five of the visitors from beyond the network
slides.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 ticket sales by origin station

points.lead: Three in five from two cities
points.text: London and Manchester send 1.46 million of the 2.45 million visitor journeys a year that start beyond the network, most of them bound for the Dales and the coast.
Nearly all of these visitors change at Leeds from an intercity train, so the connection there decides whether the trip continues by rail or by hire car.
Aligning the half-hourly Dales service with the London and Manchester arrivals cuts the average wait at Leeds from 31 minutes to 12.
The demand model credits through tickets and timed connections with 0.8 million of the 5.1 million journeys the off-peak timetable adds.

slides.title: The plan adds 11.7 million journeys a year by FY31, mostly after electrification

annotations.text: Electrified Eastern trains start to add journeys

points: Growth runs at 2.7% a year until FY28, while the Dales and Valley timetables bed in, and then at about 5% a year as electrified Eastern trains enter service and fare reform launches.
Six of the 11.7 million journeys arrive in FY30 and FY31, so the target is exposed to any slip in the power-supply upgrade due in 2029.

points.text: The contract award and the grid connection both wait on the distribution network operator's capacity study, which is now due six weeks late.
Signing the connection agreement on the study's draft findings would recover four of the six weeks, at the risk of a minor redesign of the feeder station.
All three timetable and depot milestones are on track or complete, so the 5.1 million off-peak journeys in the plan do not depend on either red row.
The fare reform consultation has not started because it is not due until October; it sits off the critical path and waits on the timetable, not the grid.

slides.title: Fare reform should follow the new timetable, not lead it
paragraphs: Cheaper off-peak fares are the obvious lever, and the one most often proposed. On Northvale's evidence they are the weaker one: lapsed riders cite the wait for the next train twice as often as the fare, and the Coast line, which already sells the cheapest off-peak day return on the network, has the lowest off-peak growth.

A fare cut on an hourly service mostly discounts trips that would have been made anyway; the Coast line's cheaper day return found exactly that, as most of its tickets went to people already travelling. The same cut on a half-hourly service reaches riders who have just been given a reason to come back, and the revenue it gives up is partly repaid by the extra journeys.

So the order matters. Run the new Dales and Valley timetables for a full year, measure who they bring back, and then design the part-time season ticket and the off-peak return around the travel patterns that result.

The cost of waiting is small. Holding fare reform until 2030 forgoes at most 0.4 million journeys a year in FY28 and FY29, the whole of what a first-mover cut would buy, and it gives the demand model a full year of half-hourly data on which to price the new products. A fare designed on a year of evidence is also easier to defend to the regulator and to passengers than one designed on a forecast.
slides.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; fare elasticity from the demand model

panel.text: Introduced first, fare reform costs £6 million a year for 0.4 million journeys; introduced second, it adds 1.6 million journeys for the same cost.

slides.title: Five decisions put Northvale on the path to 60 million journeys
items: Approve the Dales and Valley half-hourly off-peak timetables for December 2027 and May 2028.
Commit £390 million to electrify the Eastern line, with bi-mode trains as the fallback.
Hold fare reform until the new timetables have run for a year, then launch in 2030.
Hold the peak timetable and a 90% punctuality floor while train-km rise by a fifth.
Sign the grid connection on the capacity study's draft findings, recovering four of the six weeks lost.
